title: Weapons of mass decentralization - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: An essay argues the Bronze Age collapse's lasting empire-vacuum was caused by iron replacing scarce, elite-controlled bronze with a locally-minable metal that 'democratized violence,' destabilizing imperial power for centuries, and draws a direct modern parallel to how cheap drones (up to 80% of Russia-Ukraine casualties) and AI are similarly redistributing (and, for AI providers, potentially re-concentrating) the technological balance of power.

themes.theme: The puzzle: why no empire replaced the Bronze Age great powers

insights.claim: After the Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BC destroyed the Hittite, Mycenaean, and weakened Egyptian and Assyrian/Babylonian empires, the real mystery is not why they fell but why nothing like them re-emerged for centuries, since catastrophes like droughts or invasions typically cause upheaval without permanently preventing empire reconsolidation.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Reframing the puzzle from 'why did empires fall' to 'why didn't new ones rise' shifts the analytical focus toward structural, durable constraints on power concentration rather than one-off catastrophic events — a framework relevant whenever assessing whether a current power vacuum will refill quickly or persist.
insights.quote: The question is not why the Bronze Age empires fell, but why, after they fell, nothing like them returned for centuries.
insights.locator: The usual explanation points to a series

insights.claim: The average length of royal reigns across Assyria, Babylon, and Athens fell 29% after iron's adoption compared with before, and Babylon saw nearly twice as many kings in the following centuries, evidence of rising political instability.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: A 29% drop in average reign length is a concrete, comparable metric of destabilization following a military-technology shift, a benchmark for gauging how disruptive a similarly democratizing technology could be to today's power structures.
insights.quote: The average length of reigns across the sample of Assyria, Babylon, and Athens taken together falls 29 percent, and Babylon sees almost twice the number of kings in the centuries after iron adoption.
insights.locator: Ancient records allow us to build timelines

themes.theme: Bronze concentrated military power in the hands of empires

insights.claim: Bronze required tin, which was extremely scarce and had to travel thousands of miles from a handful of deposits (Afghanistan, France, Iberia, Cornwall), meaning large, complex empires could secure supply chains and stockpiles far more reliably than smaller polities, giving elites a durable military advantage.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: This establishes the general mechanism — concentrated control of a scarce input to a decisive military technology entrenches power in whoever can secure that supply chain — a pattern the essay later maps onto chip/compute control in AI.
insights.quote: elites had a major advantage in accessing the tools of violence. While smaller city-states could also get their hands on bronze, larger and more complex empires could do so more reliably.
insights.locator: This had a profound political consequence

themes.theme: Iron democratized violence by being locally abundant

insights.claim: Iron is the fourth most abundant element in Earth's crust and its ores (goethite, limonite, hematite) are visually identifiable on the surface, so peripheral communities could smelt weapons locally using bloomery furnaces, without depending on empire-controlled long-distance trade networks the way bronze required.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Local availability breaking a supply-chain chokepoint is the specific mechanism that erodes centralized power, a transferable test for evaluating whether any new technology (weapons, energy, computing) will centralize or decentralize power based on whether its key input remains scarce and controllable.
insights.quote: Since iron could be smelted locally, previously peripheral communities could arm themselves with weapons that were, for practical purposes, comparable to the weapons of the elite in the empire’s core. In contrast to bronze, iron democratized violence.
insights.locator: This new technology had momentous political

insights.claim: Iron is not actually a superior weapons material to bronze (good bronze is harder, more predictable, and easier to recycle due to its lower melting point) — iron's dominance came purely from its abundance and accessibility, not from being a better weapon.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: This is a counterintuitive but important distinction: the technology that reshapes a power balance need not be technically superior, only more accessible, a lens relevant to assessing which emerging technologies (not necessarily the most 'advanced') are most likely to disrupt existing power concentrations.
insights.quote: Iron is different: it is not a better material than bronze. Good bronze is both harder than iron and more predictable.
insights.locator: The advantage of the previous technological leap

insights.claim: Ancient writers directly linked iron to warfare and suffering: Hesiod called the Iron Age a time of endless toil and pain, Herodotus called iron 'the woe lying upon woe,' and the Philistines reportedly tried to restrict access to smiths, fearing others could easily make iron weapons.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Contemporary attempts to restrict smith access (the Philistine case) show elites recognized and tried to resist the democratizing threat of iron in real time, a historical precedent for how incumbent powers may similarly try (and fail) to gatekeep access to today's decentralizing technologies.
insights.quote: The Hebrew Bible records that the Philistines attempted to limit access to smiths as they were worried others could easily make iron weapons.
insights.locator: The effects of iron were so stark

themes.theme: Archaeological evidence of rising violence after iron

insights.claim: Skeletal remains from the Middle East show more signs of weapon-inflicted violence in the Late Bronze Age and Iron Age than in the Middle Bronze Age before iron's invention, and a battle-database study found a sharp rise in the number of battles in the century after regions adopted iron compared with the century before.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: Independent physical (skeletal) and documentary (battle-count) evidence both pointing to increased violence after iron's adoption strengthens the causal claim that technological democratization of weapons access directly increases the frequency of conflict, not just its distribution.
insights.quote: Compared with the Middle Bronze Age, before the invention of iron, skeletons from the Late Bronze Age and Iron Age show more signs of violence.
insights.locator: The archaeological record allows us to compare

themes.theme: The pattern repeats: gunpowder, nuclear weapons, drones, and AI

insights.claim: History shows a recurring cycle of centralizing and decentralizing military technologies: castles let barons resist kings until gunpowder made walls obsolete, firearms initially strengthened states while scarce but then decentralized power once cheap in the 19th-20th centuries, and nuclear weapons can act as an equalizer for a small state that achieves nuclear status.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: This framework — a technology's political effect depends on whether it changes the offense-defense balance or changes who has access to the weapon — gives a reusable analytical lens for judging the geopolitical impact of any emerging military technology.
insights.quote: Some technologies, like castles, change the offense-defense bias—whether it is easier to attack or defend. Others, like iron, change who has access to weaponry.
insights.locator: History has seen the ebb and flow

insights.claim: Drones are reportedly responsible for up to 80% of recent casualties in the Russia-Ukraine war as of 2026, with a drone costing just a few hundred dollars able to threaten a tank, artillery gun, or command post worth many times more, lowering war's cost of entry for small groups.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: An 80%-of-casualties figure and a cost-asymmetry where a few-hundred-dollar weapon can destroy multi-million-dollar hardware is direct evidence that the iron-style democratization-of-violence pattern is playing out live in the largest current conventional war, relevant to defense procurement and military-strategy decisions today.
insights.quote: drones... are reportedly responsible for up to 80 percent of recent casualties in that conflict as of 2026. A drone costing just a few hundred dollars can threaten a tank, artillery gun, or command post worth many times more.
insights.locator: A clear modern-day parallel is drones

insights.claim: AI presents an ambiguous parallel to iron: access is decentralized in that many individuals can use it (potentially to destructive effect), but AI providers retain the capacity to concentrate power because they can cut off access, centralizing control in the companies that own the models, similar to Bronze Age kings controlling tin stockpiles.
insights.speaker: Works in Progress
insights.so_what: This flags a live, unresolved policy question: whether AI ultimately decentralizes power (like iron) or re-concentrates it in a handful of model-owning companies (like Bronze Age tin control) depends on decisions about access and export control being made right now, making this a framework investors and policymakers should apply directly to current AI-governance debates.
insights.quote: AI providers have the capacity to concentrate power. Access can be cut off, centralizing the use of AI in the hands of the companies that own it... similar to the advantage enjoyed by Bronze Age kings who controlled stores of tin.
insights.locator: Another parallel can perhaps be seen in AI
